desc:
Choose exactly k elements of nums that are the k largest. When several elements share a value that sits on the boundary, prefer the one with the smaller index.

Return the chosen values in the order in which they appear in nums.

nums = [5, 2, 7, 2, 9, 7], k = 3
largest three: 9 (index 4), 7 (index 2), 7 (index 5)
answer = [7, 9, 7]

nums = [3, 5, 3, 1], k = 2
largest: 5, then one of the two 3s -> take the earlier one (index 0)
answer = [3, 5]
hints: Sorting the whole array loses the original order, but you could sort indices instead of values.
Find the k-th largest value t. Everything larger than t is surely chosen, and some of the elements equal to t are chosen as well. How many?
Count how many elements are strictly greater than t; the remaining k - that slots go to the first elements equal to t. Then one left-to-right pass collects the answer.
editorial: Let t be the k-th largest value (counting duplicates). Every element greater than t must be in the answer, and exactly need = k - (count of elements greater than t) elements equal to t are needed. The tie rule says the earliest ones win.
Walk through the array from left to right: take x if x > t, or if x == t and need > 0 (then decrement need). The output is automatically in original order.
Finding t by sorting costs O(n log n); quickselect finds it in expected O(n). The final pass is O(n).
